title: Reverse-KL Policy Distillation: Statistical Guarantees and Limits

paper.title: Reverse-KL Policy Distillation: Statistical Guarantees and Limits
paper.abstract:
Abstract Reverse Kullback–Leibler (KL) distillation has shown empirical promise for training
language models, but its statistical guarantees and limits remain poorly understood.
In particular, the effects of two design choices remain unclear: Does access to the teacher’s full action distribution provide an advantage over observing only the probability it assigns to the sampled action? Must training trajectories come from the student (online distillation), or can teacher-generated trajectories (offline distillation) suffice? Our work takes a first step toward understanding the theory underlying these questions. We study the sample complexity of online reverse-KL distillation under two feedback models: the teacher reveals either its full action distribution or only the probability of the student -generated action. We establish minimax bounds for the former and show that substantially more data may be required for the latter.
In contrast, offline reverse-KL distillation can attain the same minimax rate whether the teacher reveals its full distribution or only its probability of the teacher -generated action.
The key distinction is that teacher-generated actions themselves reveal the teacher’s preferences, while queries at student-selected actions can leave those preferences unobserved. This highlights an additional statistical challenge for online distillation compared to offline distillation. These statistical guarantees do not follow simply from optimizing standard distillation objectives: our lower bounds show that common online objectives can fail when candidates are evaluated only on past student-generated trajectories.
We develop trajectory-loss and importance-ratio truncation techniques together with policy-space learning to achieve optimal online distillation guarantees.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Policy distillation compresses a teacher into a student that may lack the capacity to reproduce the teacher’s behavior in full. The choice of divergence therefore matters. Forward Kullback–Leibler (KL) divergence (i.e., KL \operatorname{KL} (teacher ∥ \| student)) encourages the student to cover the teacher’s full range of responses. Reverse KL (i.e., KL \operatorname{KL} (student ∥ \| teacher)) instead allows a limited-capacity student to concentrate on teacher behaviors it can represent, while discouraging responses that are unlikely under the teacher. Reverse KL has shown empirical promise in on-policy distillation for large language models (LLMs), where the student generates responses and learns from the teacher’s action probability at the observed state ( Gu et al., 2024 ; Agarwal et al., 2024 ; Lu and Thinking Machines Lab, 2025 ) . Although the empirical results are promising, the optimal statistical guarantees for reverse-KL learning remain unclear. The statistical question depends first on what information the teacher provides. Some distillation methods only use the teacher’s probability on student-generated actions ( Lu and Thinking Machines Lab, 2025 ) , whereas recent studies report benefits from access to the teacher’s full action distribution ( Li et al., 2026b ; Yu et al., 2026 ; Fu et al., 2026 ) . Whether this richer form of teacher feedback improves statistical efficiency, and by how much, remains open. Moreover, reverse KL is evaluated under the student’s distribution, so training typically uses student-generated responses. It is therefore unclear whether learning from offline teacher-generated data can match or even improve on the statistical guarantees attainable from online student rollouts. To answer these questions, we study sequence-level reverse-KL learning with a student policy class that may not contain the teacher, allowing for misspecification . Our framework distinguishes two aspects of the learning process: who generates the training trajectories and what information the teacher provides along them. The trajectories come either from student policies chosen adaptively by the learner in the online setting, or from the teacher in the offline setting. With either data source, the teacher may reveal its entire action distribution at each visited state ( full feedback ) or only the probability of the observed action ( action feedback ). Across these four settings, we study how closely a learner can match the best student in its policy class for a given number of training trajectories. We give a rather complete picture for this problem. With full feedback, we establish the minimax-optimal guarantees for reverse-KL learning under a relative second-moment assumption. For the online setting, we first show that common local distillation losses can be suboptimal. These objectives, motivated by DAgger and on-policy distillation ( Ross et al., 2011 ; Lu and Thinking Machines Lab, 2025 ) , evaluate candidate policy on states generated by the rollout policies, including state that a candidate itself would rarely visit, which can distort policy rankings. Our algorithm ( Algorithm 1 ) corrects this mismatch by reweighting the observed prefix to account for each policy’s own generation behavior, attaining the optimal guarantee ( Section 3 ). For the offline setting, we develop a new algorithm ( Equation 12 ) that attains the same optimal guarantee from teacher-generated trajectories. With action feedback only, online learning can require substantially more samples than with full feedback ( Section 3.4 ). Yet under a trajectory likelihood-ratio bound, offline learning with action feedback can still obtain a comparable guarantee to full feedback learning ( Sections 3.4 and 4 ). These results show that richer feedback can improve online sample efficiency, while surprisingly optimal reverse-KL learning need not require online interaction. Formally, let π ⋆ \pi^{\star} be the teacher policy, Π \Pi be the student policy class, and P π P^{\pi} the sequence distribution generated by π \pi . Our guarantees take the form KL ( P π ^ ∥ P π ⋆ ) ≤ C app min π ∈ Π KL ( P π ∥ P π ⋆ ) + C est log ⁡ ( | Π | / δ ) T \operatorname{KL}(P^{\widehat{\pi}}\|P^{\pi^{\star}})\leq C_{\rm app}\min_{\pi\in\Pi}\operatorname{KL}(P^{\pi}\|P^{\pi^{\star}})+C_{\rm est}\frac{\log(|\Pi|/\delta)}{T} with probability at least 1 − δ 1-\delta , using T T complete episodes and returning π ^ ∈ Π \widehat{\pi}\in\Pi . Here C app C_{\rm app} (approximation factor) measures the approximation cost of competing with the best available student, and C est C_{\rm est} (estimation factor) controls the estimation error. At the minimax scale of C est C_{\rm est} , we characterize the smallest attainable C app C_{\rm app} . Table 1 summarizes the guarantees and separations. The assumptions hold for every π \pi and feasible trajectory τ \tau . The trajectory likelihood-ratio condition is stronger and implies the relative second moment condition with B = 4 ​ ( B ∞ + 1 ) B=4(B_{\infty}+1) ( Lemma D.1 ).

sections.heading: Related work.
sections.text: Our closest theoretical predecessors Rohatgi et al. (2025) and Xu et al. (2026b) also study imitation learning under misspecification. Rohatgi et al. (2025) obtain constant approximation and estimation coefficients for learning trajectory Hellinger distance with computationally inefficient algorithms, and show that standard next-token prediction approaches (e.g. cross-entropy loss) must suffer an Ω ⁡ ( H ) \Omega(H) approximation factor where H H is the learning horizon. Xu et al. (2026b) establish a constant approximation factor for learning forward KL divergence under standard cross-entropy loss, but the estimation error scales with a boundedness factor. Both papers only study offline learning from teacher trajectories with action feedback. We study reverse-KL learning in both online and offline settings and characterize the statistical advantage of full feedback over action feedback. Appendix A provides further discussion of related work.

sections.heading: Setting.
sections.text: We consider a reward-free Markov decision process with horizon H ≥ 1 H\geq 1 , discrete state space 𝒮 \mathcal{S} , action set 𝒜 \mathcal{A} , initial state distribution μ \mu , and transition kernel 𝖯 h ( ⋅ ∣ s , a ) \mathsf{P}_{h}(\cdot\mid s,a) . A Markov policy π = ( π h ) h = 1 H \pi=(\pi_{h})_{h=1}^{H} consists of maps π h : 𝒮 → Δ ⁡ ( 𝒜 ) \pi_{h}:\mathcal{S}\to\Delta(\mathcal{A}) , where Δ ⁡ ( 𝒜 ) = { p ∈ [ 0 , 1 ] | 𝒜 | : ∑ a ∈ 𝒜 p ⁡ ( a ) = 1 } \Delta(\mathcal{A})=\{p\in[0,1]^{|\mathcal{A}|}:\sum_{a\in\mathcal{A}}p(a)=1\} is the probability simplex over actions. We write π h ​ ( a ∣ s ) \pi_{h}(a\mid s) for the probability assigned to action a a at state s s . Let s h ∈ 𝒮 s_{h}\in\mathcal{S} and a h ∈ 𝒜 a_{h}\in\mathcal{A} denote the state and action at step h h . Under π \pi , an episode generates a trajectory τ = ( s 1 , a 1 , … , s H , a H ) ∈ 𝒯 = ( 𝒮 × 𝒜 ) H \tau=(s_{1},a_{1},\ldots,s_{H},a_{H})\in\mathcal{T}=(\mathcal{S}\times\mathcal{A})^{H} by sampling s 1 ∼ μ s_{1}\sim\mu , a h ∼ π h ( ⋅ ∣ s h ) a_{h}\sim\pi_{h}(\cdot\mid s_{h}) , and, for h < H h<H , s h + 1 ∼ 𝖯 h ( ⋅ ∣ s h , a h ) s_{h+1}\sim\mathsf{P}_{h}(\cdot\mid s_{h},a_{h}) . We write P π P^{\pi} for the trajectory distribution under policy π \pi , so P π ​ ( τ ) = μ ⁡ ( s 1 ) ​ ∏ h = 1 H π h ​ ( a h ∣ s h ) ​ ∏ h = 1 H − 1 𝖯 h ​ ( s h + 1 ∣ s h , a h ) . P^{\pi}(\tau)=\mu(s_{1})\prod_{h=1}^{H}\pi_{h}(a_{h}\mid s_{h})\prod_{h=1}^{H-1}\mathsf{P}_{h}(s_{h+1}\mid s_{h},a_{h}). Let ξ h = ( s 1 , a 1 , … , s h − 1 , a h − 1 , s h ) \xi_{h}=(s_{1},a_{1},\ldots,s_{h-1},a_{h-1},s_{h}) denote the prefix before action a h a_{h} . Its probability under π \pi is P π ​ ( ξ h ) = μ ⁡ ( s 1 ) ​ ∏ j = 1 h − 1 π j ​ ( a j ∣ s j ) ​ 𝖯 j ​ ( s j + 1 ∣ s j , a j ) . P^{\pi}(\xi_{h})=\mu(s_{1})\prod_{j=1}^{h-1}\pi_{j}(a_{j}\mid s_{j})\mathsf{P}_{j}(s_{j+1}\mid s_{j},a_{j}). The empty product equals one when h = 1 h=1 . The learner is given a finite policy class Π \Pi and seeks to imitate a fixed teacher π ⋆ \pi^{\star} . Define the local reverse KL between policy π \pi and π ⋆ \pi^{\star} at state s s and step h h by k h ( s ; π ) = KL ( π h ( ⋅ ∣ s ) ∥ π h ⋆ ( ⋅ ∣ s ) ) k_{h}(s;\pi)=\operatorname{KL}(\pi_{h}(\cdot\mid s)\|\pi_{h}^{\star}(\cdot\mid s)) . Our target is the trajectory reverse-KL risk , whose chain-rule decomposition is L ( π ) := KL ( P π ∥ P π ⋆ ) = 𝔼 P π [ ∑ h = 1 H k h ( s h ; π ) ] . L(\pi):=\operatorname{KL}(P^{\pi}\|P^{\pi^{\star}})=\mathbb{E}_{P^{\pi}}\big[\sum_{h=1}^{H}k_{h}(s_{h};\pi)\big]. Let L ⋆ = min π ∈ Π ⁡ L ⁡ ( π ) L^{\star}=\min_{\pi\in\Pi}L(\pi) . The setting is realizable when π ⋆ ∈ Π \pi^{\star}\in\Pi , giving L ⋆ = 0 L^{\star}=0 , and agnostic when the teacher need not belong to the class.

sections.heading: Observation models.
sections.text: With a budget of T T complete episodes, we consider four observation models (see Table 1 ) that differ in their trajectory source and teacher feedback : • Trajectory source: In the online setting, at each round t ∈ [ T ] t\in[T] , the learner selects π t ∈ Π \pi_{t}\in\Pi based on past observations and executes it for a complete episode, obtaining τ t ∼ P π t \tau_{t}\sim P^{\pi_{t}} . In the offline setting, the learner receives independent teacher trajectories τ t ⋆ ∼ P π ⋆ \tau_{t}^{\star}\sim P^{\pi^{\star}} for t ∈ [ T ] t\in[T] . • Teacher feedback: At each visited state s h s_{h} , the learner receives one of two forms of teacher feedback. Full feedback reveals the teacher’s entire action distribution π h ⋆ ( ⋅ ∣ s h ) \pi_{h}^{\star}(\cdot\mid s_{h}) , whereas action feedback reveals only the probability π h ⋆ ​ ( a h ∣ s h ) \pi_{h}^{\star}(a_{h}\mid s_{h}) assigned to the observed action a h a_{h} . Either feedback model can accompany online or offline trajectories, and no feedback is available at unvisited states.

sections.heading: Boundedness assumptions.
sections.text: Our full-feedback guarantees hold under a relative second-moment condition. For action feedback, we use a stronger trajectory likelihood-ratio bound. Assumption 2.1 (Relative second-moment bound) . There exists B ≥ 1 B\geq 1 such that, for every π ∈ Π \pi\in\Pi , 𝔼 τ ∼ P π [ ( ∑ h = 1 H KL ( π h ( ⋅ ∣ s h ) ∥ π h ⋆ ( ⋅ ∣ s h ) ) ) 2 ] ≤ B KL ( P π ∥ P π ⋆ ) < ∞ . \mathbb{E}_{\tau\sim P^{\pi}}\!\left[\left(\sum_{h=1}^{H}\operatorname{KL}\!\left(\pi_{h}(\cdot\mid s_{h})\,\middle\|\,\pi_{h}^{\star}(\cdot\mid s_{h})\right)\right)^{2}\right]\leq B\,\operatorname{KL}(P^{\pi}\|P^{\pi^{\star}})<\infty. By the KL chain rule, the average cumulative local KL under P π P^{\pi} equals the trajectory divergence KL ( P π ∥ P π ⋆ ) \operatorname{KL}(P^{\pi}\|P^{\pi^{\star}}) . Assumption 2.1 thus imposes a Bernstein-type moment condition , the second moment is controlled linearly by the mean under each candidate policy’s own trajectory distribution. Intuitively, trajectories with cumulative local KL much larger than B B can contribute only a small fraction of the average reverse KL. This condition is weaker than several uniform boundedness assumptions. For example, a uniform local KL bound k h ​ ( s , π ) ≤ G k_{h}(s;\pi)\leq G for all h , s , π h,s,\pi implies Assumption 2.1 with B = max ⁡ { 1 , H ​ G } B=\max\{1,HG\} . The trajectory likelihood-ratio bound in Assumption 2.2 below also implies Assumption 2.1 , with B = 4 ​ ( B ∞ + 1 ) B=4(B_{\infty}+1) . Section D.1 provides the precise implications and proofs. Let 𝒯 env \mathcal{T}_{\rm env} denote the set of environment-feasible trajectories τ = ( s 1 : H , a 1 : H ) \tau=(s_{1:H},a_{1:H}) satisfying μ ⁡ ( s 1 ) ​ ∏ h = 1 H − 1 𝖯 h ​ ( s h + 1 ∣ s h , a h ) > 0 \mu(s_{1})\prod_{h=1}^{H-1}\mathsf{P}_{h}(s_{h+1}\mid s_{h},a_{h})>0 . Assumption 2.2 gives trajectory likelihood-ratio bound. Assumption 2.2 (Trajectory likelihood-ratio bound) . There is B ∞ > 1 B_{\infty}>1 such that P π ​ ( τ ) ≤ e B ∞ ​ P π ⋆ ​ ( τ ) P^{\pi}(\tau)\leq e^{B_{\infty}}P^{\pi^{\star}}(\tau) for every π ∈ Π \pi\in\Pi and τ ∈ 𝒯 env \tau\in\mathcal{T}_{\rm env} . The local bound π h ​ ( a ∣ s ) ≤ e G ​ π h ⋆ ​ ( a ∣ s ) \pi_{h}(a\mid s)\leq e^{G}\pi_{h}^{\star}(a\mid s) implies trajectory-level bound P π ​ ( τ ) ≤ e H ​ G ​ P π ⋆ ​ ( τ ) P^{\pi}(\tau)\leq e^{HG}P^{\pi^{\star}}(\tau) . Thus, B B and B ∞ B_{\infty} may themselves grow with H H , so the absence of an explicit horizon factor in our guarantees does not imply horizon independence. Like our Assumption 2.2 , Assumption 1 of Xu et al. (2026b) also bounds likelihood ratios, but in the opposite direction P π ⋆ ​ ( τ ) / P π ​ ( τ ) P^{\pi^{\star}}(\tau)/P^{\pi}(\tau) rather than our P π ​ ( τ ) / P π ⋆ ​ ( τ ) P^{\pi}(\tau)/P^{\pi^{\star}}(\tau) . Their assumption requires every student to cover the teacher for a forward-KL objective, whereas our Assumption 2.2 requires the teacher to cover every student for a reverse KL objective. Teacher coverage is more natural in many cases because a limited-capacity student may concentrate on teacher-supported behaviors without representing the teacher’s entire range of behaviors.

sections.heading: Approximation error and estimation error.
sections.text: Following Rohatgi et al. (2025) and Xu et al. (2026b) , we seek a learner that returns π ^ ∈ Π \widehat{\pi}\in\Pi such that, with probability at least 1 − δ 1-\delta , L ⁡ ( π ^ ) ≤ C app ​ L ⋆ ⏟ approximation error + C est ​ log ⁡ ( | Π | / δ ) T ⏟ estimation error . L(\widehat{\pi})\leq\underbrace{C_{\rm app}L^{\star}}_{\text{approximation error}}+\underbrace{C_{\rm est}\frac{\log(|\Pi|/\delta)}{T}}_{\text{estimation error}}. The coefficients may depend on B , B ∞ , H , | Π | , | 𝒜 | B,B_{\infty},H,|\Pi|,|\mathcal{A}| and the observation model. Here L ⋆ L^{\star} is the smallest risk achievable by any student in Π \Pi . The coefficient C app C_{\rm app} measures how closely the learner competes with this best-in-class risk. The coefficient C est C_{\rm est} scales the estimation term log ⁡ ( | Π | / δ ) / T \log(|\Pi|/\delta)/T , determining how many episodes are needed for accurate learning. We fix C est C_{\rm est} at its minimax-optimal order and characterize the smallest attainable C app C_{\rm app} .

sections.heading: 3 Online learning from student trajectories
sections.text: In this section, we study online reverse-KL learning, where student policies generate trajectories and the teacher reveals its full action distribution at each visited state. We first show that exact refitting with common distillation losses can fail because it evaluates candidates under mismatched visitation distributions. We then introduce an algorithm that corrects this mismatch and attains the optimal guarantee.

sections.heading: 3.1 Why common objectives can fail
sections.text: A natural approach fits each new student to the teacher’s predictions on states visited during training, as in DAgger-style refitting and the local objectives used in on-policy distillation ( Ross et al., 2011 ; Agarwal et al., 2024 ) . At round t t , the current student π t \pi_{t} generates a batch of complete trajectories with full teacher feedback. Let 𝒟 t \mathcal{D}_{t} contain all trajectories observed so far. The learner chooses the next student by π t + 1 ∈ arg ​ min π ∈ Π ⁡ Q t ​ ( π , 𝒟 t ) . \pi_{t+1}\in\operatorname*{arg\,min}_{\pi\in\Pi}Q_{t}(\pi;\mathcal{D}_{t}). (1) The objective may use any nonempty subset of 𝒟 t \mathcal{D}_{t} , including only the latest batch, or assign arbitrary nonnegative weights to complete trajectories. These choices may depend on the observed data but must be the same for all candidates. If π t \pi_{t} is already an empirical minimizer, the learner retains it. For example, reverse-KL refitting minimizes a weighted sum of ∑ h = 1 H k h ​ ( s h , π ) \sum_{h=1}^{H}k_{h}(s_{h};\pi) over the selected trajectories. Such local reverse-KL losses appear in generalized knowledge distillation and recent on-policy distillation studies ( Agarwal et al., 2024 ; Li et al., 2026a ) . Other choices include forward KL, mixtures of the two KL directions, and clipped KL losses ( Lin et al., 2020 ; Wu et al., 2025 ; Zhao et al., 2026 ) . Section B.1 specifies the allowed losses and transformations. The result concerns exact refitting with these objectives, not every gradient update used in the cited methods. Changing which trajectories are retained does not necessarily correct the visitation mismatch. A candidate π \pi is still evaluated at states visited by the rollout policies, rather than according to how often π \pi itself would visit those states. In the construction below, a constant-probability event makes every observed trajectory favor a high-risk policy, so selecting a different subset cannot improve the empirical ranking. Proposition 3.1 . For every sufficiently large B B , there is an H = 2 H=2 , | Π | = 2 |\Pi|=2 instance satisfying Assumptions 2.1 and 2.2 with B ∞ = 2 ​ B B_{\infty}=2B and L ⋆ ≤ e − Ω ⁡ ( B ) L^{\star}\leq e^{-\Omega(B)} on which the refitting rules above fail. Under uniform random initialization, after T = Θ ⁡ ( B 3 ) T=\Theta(B^{3}) episodes, the policy returned by the final refit has risk Ω ⁡ ( B ) \Omega(B) with constant probability, even with adaptive selection and weighting of past trajectories. The construction has a high-risk policy π bad \pi_{\rm bad} that frequently visits a state where the near-optimal policy π good \pi_{\rm good} has a large local loss. Although π good \pi_{\rm good} rarely reaches this state itself, its loss on trajectories from π bad \pi_{\rm bad} makes it look worse. With constant probability, random initialization selects π bad \pi_{\rm bad} and every subsequent refit retains it, even if past data are discarded. Our algorithm reduces the influence of prefixes that the evaluated policy would rarely reach.

sections.heading: 3.2 Correcting visitation mismatch
sections.text: Suppose π t \pi_{t} generates a trajectory ( s 1 : H , a 1 : H ) (s_{1:H},a_{1:H}) at round t ∈ [ T ] t\in[T] . Full teacher feedback reveals the local loss k h ​ ( s h , π ) k_{h}(s_{h};\pi) for every candidate π \pi at each visited state, but the visited prefixes are sampled according to π t \pi_{t} rather than π \pi . Writing ξ h = ( s 1 , a 1 , … , s h − 1 , a h − 1 , s h ) \xi_{h}=(s_{1},a_{1},\ldots,s_{h-1},a_{h-1},s_{h}) for the prefix before action a h a_{h} , standard importance weighting multiplies a loss at ξ h \xi_{h} by P π ​ ( ξ h ) / P π t ​ ( ξ h ) P^{\pi}(\xi_{h})/P^{\pi_{t}}(\xi_{h}) . Under rollouts from π t \pi_{t} , this changes its expected coefficient from P π t ​ ( ξ h ) P^{\pi_{t}}(\xi_{h}) to P π ​ ( ξ h ) P^{\pi}(\xi_{h}) . However, the importance ratio can be arbitrarily large when a prefix is rare under π t \pi_{t} , making the resulting estimate highly sensitive to rare observations. We therefore clip the weight at one, giving min ⁡ { 1 , P π ​ ( ξ h ) / P π t ​ ( ξ h ) } \min\{1,P^{\pi}(\xi_{h})/P^{\pi_{t}}(\xi_{h})\} . Any loss attached to ξ h \xi_{h} then enters the expectation with coefficient P π t ​ ( ξ h ) ​ min ⁡ { 1 , P π ​ ( ξ h ) / P π t ​ ( ξ h ) } = min ⁡ { P π ​ ( ξ h ) , P π t ​ ( ξ h ) } P^{\pi_{t}}(\xi_{h})\min\{1,P^{\pi}(\xi_{h})/P^{\pi_{t}}(\xi_{h})\}=\min\{P^{\pi}(\xi_{h}),P^{\pi_{t}}(\xi_{h})\} . Thus, a prefix ξ h \xi_{h} that π \pi visits less often than π t \pi_{t} is downweighted to P π ​ ( ξ h ) P^{\pi}(\xi_{h}) , whereas a prefix that π \pi visits more often is not amplified beyond P π t ​ ( ξ h ) P^{\pi_{t}}(\xi_{h}) . The ratio can be computed as P π ​ ( ξ h ) / P π t ​ ( ξ h ) = ∏ u < h π u ​ ( a u | s u ) / π t , u ​ ( a u | s u ) P^{\pi}(\xi_{h})/P^{\pi_{t}}(\xi_{h})=\prod_{u<h}\pi_{u}(a_{u}|s_{u})/\pi_{t,u}(a_{u}|s_{u}) because the transition probabilities cancel. Although each importance ratio is clipped, the local KL losses along a trajectory can still sum to a large value. We therefore consider the clipped cumulative local loss min ⁡ { 1 , ∑ h = 1 H k h ​ ( s h , π ) } \min\!\big\{1,\sum_{h=1}^{H}k_{h}(s_{h};\pi)\big\} . To combine this trajectory-level clipping with the step-dependent prefix weights, we decompose the clipped total loss into increments. Specifically, let e h ​ ( ξ h , π ) e_{h}(\xi_{h};\pi) be the increase caused by adding the local loss at step h h , e h ​ ( ξ h , π ) = min ⁡ { 1 , ∑ u = 1 h k u ​ ( s u , π ) } − min ⁡ { 1 , ∑ u = 1 h − 1 k u ​ ( s u , π ) } . e_{h}(\xi_{h};\pi)=\min\!\left\{1,\sum_{u=1}^{h}k_{u}(s_{u};\pi)\right\}-\min\!\left\{1,\sum_{u=1}^{h-1}k_{u}(s_{u};\pi)\right\}. (2) The increments e h ​ ( ξ h , π ) e_{h}(\xi_{h};\pi) are nonnegative and ∑ h = 1 H e h ​ ( ξ h , π ) = min ⁡ { 1 , ∑ h = 1 H k h ​ ( s h , π ) } ≤ 1 \sum_{h=1}^{H}e_{h}(\xi_{h};\pi)=\min\!\big\{1,\sum_{h=1}^{H}k_{h}(s_{h};\pi)\big\}\leq 1 . The two clipping operations reduce the influence of rare, high-loss observations, but they also discard information about the original reverse-KL risk. To quantify what remains, let L ¯ ​ ( π ) := 𝔼 P π ​ [ ∑ h = 1 H e h ​ ( ξ h , π ) ] \overline{L}(\pi):=\mathbb{E}_{P^{\pi}}\big[\sum_{h=1}^{H}e_{h}(\xi_{h};\pi)\big] denote policy π \pi ’s expected clipped loss. First, under Assumption 2.1 , clipping incurs a factor O ⁡ ( B ) O(B) , L ¯ ​ ( π ) ≤ L ⁡ ( π ) ≲ B ​ L ¯ ​ ( π ) . \overline{L}(\pi)\leq L(\pi)\lesssim B\,\overline{L}(\pi). (3) Thus, controlling the clipped loss L ¯ ​ ( π ) \overline{L}(\pi) suffices to control sequence risk L ⁡ ( π ) L(\pi) , at a cost of B B ( Lemma D.2 ). Second, the rollout policy π t \pi_{t} may rarely visit prefixes that are important to π \pi . sections.heading: 3.4 The Limitation of Action Feedback in the Online Setting
sections.text: Algorithm 1 uses the teacher’s full action distribution to evaluate the local KL losses of every π ∈ Π \pi\in\Pi . With action feedback, the learner only observes the teacher’s probability on its chosen action, while the probabilities of other actions remain unobserved. The following lower bound shows that this missing information can significantly increase the sample requirement of any learner, even in the realizable setting. Theorem 3.5 (Online action-feedback lower bound) . For a sufficiently large T T , every online learner returning a policy π ^ ∈ Π \widehat{\pi}\in\Pi with action feedback from the teacher has a realizable instance satisfying Assumption 2.2 , on which L ⁡ ( π ^ ) = Ω ~ ​ ( min ⁡ { | 𝒜 | , | Π | , e B ∞ } ​ B ∞ ​ log ⁡ | Π | T ) L(\widehat{\pi})=\widetilde{\Omega}\!\left(\min\{|\mathcal{A}|,|\Pi|,e^{B_{\infty}}\}\frac{B_{\infty}\log|\Pi|}{T}\right) with probability at least 1 / 4 1/4 . Compared with the full-feedback guarantee in Theorem 3.2 , this lower bound requires an additional factor of min ⁡ { | 𝒜 | , | Π | , e B ∞ } \min\{|\mathcal{A}|,|\Pi|,e^{B_{\infty}}\} in the estimation error even in the realizable setting. Full feedback therefore provides a statistical advantage over action feedback in the online learning setting.

sections.heading: 4 Offline learning from teacher trajectories

Thus, the reduction from Hellinger to reverse KL learning is minimax optimal in this setting. Proposition 4.3 and Theorem 3.5 show that, under Assumption 2.2 , offline action-feedback learning can require exponentially fewer episodes than online action-feedback learning in the worst case.

sections.heading: 5 Conclusion
sections.text: We characterize how data source and teacher feedback shape reverse-KL learning under misspecification. For the online learning setting, we show the failure of common empirical algorithms and provide the first algorithm achieving the optimal guarantee under full feedback and a relative second-moment condition. We further show that full feedback can significantly improve online sample efficiency over action feedback. For the offline setting, we also establish algorithms with tight bounds, demonstrating that under a trajectory likelihood-ratio bound, teacher trajectories can avoid the additional sample cost of online learning with action feedback. Future work includes developing and empirically evaluating practical distillation algorithms based on our prefix reweighting and trajectory clipping mechanism, and determining the optimal statistical guarantees achievable by computationally efficient learners.

sections.heading: Offline imitation learning theory
sections.text: Offline imitation learning asks what can be learned from a fixed set of expert demonstrations without further interaction. In the realizable setting, classical analyses of zero-one-loss behavior cloning relate action-prediction errors to compounding errors in task performance [ Ross and Bagnell, 2010 ] . Rajaraman et al. [2020] characterize minimax task-performance guarantees in finite-state MDPs, showing that error compounding can be unavoidable when dynamics are unknown. With known dynamics and a deterministic expert, improved dependence on the horizon is possible [ Rajaraman et al., 2021 ] . For general policy classes under realizability, Foster et al. [2024] show that log-loss behavior cloning admits horizon-free guarantees when the cumulative reward range and policy-class complexity are controlled. Additional offline data provide another source of information: MILO learns a dynamics model from auxiliary transition data and mitigates covariate shift when those data sufficiently cover the expert’s behavior [ Chang et al., 2021 ] . Our offline learners instead use teacher trajectories and the specified probability feedback, without auxiliary transition data. When the student policy class is not expressive enough to cover the teacher, the question becomes how closely a learner can compete with the best available policy. A common target is an oracle bound of the form D ⁡ ( π ^ , π ⋆ ) ≤ C app ​ min π ∈ Π ⁡ D ⁡ ( π , π ⋆ ) + C est ​ log ⁡ ( | Π | / δ ) / T D(\widehat{\pi};\pi^{\star})\leq C_{\rm app}\min_{\pi\in\Pi}D(\pi;\pi^{\star})+C_{\rm est}\log(|\Pi|/\delta)/T where D ⁡ ( ⋅ , ⋅ ) D(\cdot;\cdot) can be any distance measure. For trajectory-level Hellinger distance, Rohatgi et al. [2025] give an offline estimator with constant approximation and estimation coefficients, while establishing an Ω ⁡ ( H ) \Omega(H) approximation barrier for a broad class of next-token methods. Xu et al. [2026b] study trajectory-level forward KL divergence, obtaining constant-factor approximation error with Θ ⁡ ( H ​ G ) \Theta(HG) estimation error where sup π ∈ Π sup h ∈ [ H ] sup s h log ⁡ π h ⋆ ​ ( x h ∣ s h ) π h ​ ( x h ∣ s h ) ≤ G . \sup_{\pi\in\Pi}\sup_{h\in[H]}\sup_{s_{h}}\log\frac{\pi_{h}^{\star}(x_{h}\mid s_{h})}{\pi_{h}(x_{h}\mid s_{h})}\leq G. Both Rohatgi et al. [2025] and Xu et al. [2026b] study offline learning with action feedback. In the same setting, we study reverse KL learning and show that C app , C est = Θ ⁡ ( B ∞ ) C_{\rm app},C_{\rm est}=\Theta(B_{\infty}) under Assumption 2.2 . Due to the different directions in forward and reverse KL, we assume the teacher can cover any student, whereas Xu et al. [2026b] assumes any student can cover the teacher. Teacher coverage is more natural for distillation because a limited-capacity student may concentrate on teacher-supported behaviors without representing the teacher’s entire range of behaviors.

sections.heading: Interactive imitation learning
sections.text: A student may visit states rarely represented in teacher demonstrations, especially after making a mistake [ Ross and Bagnell, 2010 ] . DAgger obtains expert supervision on these states and reduces imitation to no-regret online learning [ Ross et al., 2011 ] . Li and Zhang [2024] give an oracle-efficient agnostic algorithm with access to exploratory state samples. Its comparator measures local imitation error on states visited during training; ours evaluates each candidate under its own trajectory law. Thus a small online regret alone does not imply our reverse-KL oracle bound. Several works identify conditions under which interaction improves imitation-learning performance. Espinosa-Dice et al. [2025] avoid quadratic error compounding under a completeness condition on the policy class. Zhang et al. [2026] identify an offline information bottleneck under misspecification even at horizon one. Sriraman et al. [2026] establish an exponential benefit from interaction with a noisy expert when performance is measured against a clean expert. Viano et al. [2026] obtain efficient on-policy imitation when the expert’s Q-function, rather than its policy, is realizable. These guarantees concern different targets and assumptions from our comparison of online and offline reverse-KL learning rates.

sections.heading: Language-model distillation
sections.text: Building on knowledge and policy distillation [ Hinton et al., 2015 , Rusu et al., 2016 ] , language-model distillation can use teacher-generated responses [ Kim and Rush, 2016 ] or student-generated responses [ Lin et al., 2020 , Agarwal et al., 2024 , Li et al., 2026a ] , with forward KL and reverse KL as common losses. Beyond the standard losses, Wu et al. [2025] propose an adaptive combination of these two losses. Ko et al. [2024] propose skew KL losses that compare a distribution with a mixture of teacher and student distributions, while Ko et al. [2025] use a contrastive objective to increase the likelihood of teacher responses and decrease that of student responses. Gu et al. [2024] develop policy-gradient updates for sequence-level reverse KL, using returns based on accumulated future teacher-to-student log likelihood ratios. These returns allow later predictions to influence updates to earlier actions. The feedback available at each training recipe is a separate choice. Lu and Thinking Machines Lab [2025] use teacher probabilities for sampled tokens, Xu et al. [2026a] use full next-token distributions, and Fu et al. [2026] , Yu et al. [2026] incorporate information about teacher-preferred alternatives. Our full-versus-action-feedback comparison isolates the statistical value of the available information by comparing the best attainable rates under each feedback model.

text: Reverse-KL Policy Distillation: Statistical Guarantees and Limits Skip to main content Report GitHub Issue × Title: Content selection saved. Describe the issue below: Description: Why HTML? Report Issue Back to Abstract Download PDF Contents Reading mode Colour theme License: arXiv.org perpetual non-exclusive license arXiv:2610.30844v1 [cs.LG] 22 Oct 2026 Reverse-KL Policy Distillation: Statistical Guarantees and Limits Haolin Liu Affiliation: University of Virginia Email: srs8rh@virginia.edu Chen-Yu Wei Affiliation: University of Virginia Email: chenyu.wei@virginia.edu Julian Zimmert Affiliation: Google Research / Affiliation: National Taiwan University Email: zimmert@google.com Abstract Reverse Kullback–Leibler (KL) distillation has shown empirical promise for training language models, but its statistical guarantees and limits remain poorly understood. In particular, the effects of two design choices remain unclear: Does access to the teacher’s full action distribution provide an advantage over observing only the probability it assigns to the sampled action? Must training trajectories come from the student (online distillation), or can teacher-generated trajectories (offline distillation) suffice? Our work takes a first step toward understanding the theory underlying these questions. We study the sample complexity of online reverse-KL distillation under two feedback models: the teacher reveals either its full action distribution or only the probability of the student -generated action. We establish minimax bounds for the former and show that substantially more data may be required for the latter. In contrast, offline reverse-KL distillation can attain the same minimax rate whether the teacher reveals its full distribution or only its probability of the teacher -generated action. The key distinction is that teacher-generated actions themselves reveal the teacher’s preferences, while queries at student-selected actions can leave those preferences unobserved. This highlights an additional statistical challenge for online distillation compared to offline distillation. These statistical guarantees do not follow simply from optimizing standard distillation objectives: our lower bounds show that common online objectives can fail when candidates are evaluated only on past student-generated trajectories. We develop trajectory-loss and importance-ratio truncation techniques together with policy-space learning to achieve optimal online distillation guarantees. 1 Introduction Policy distillation compresses a teacher into a student that may lack the capacity to reproduce the teacher’s behavior in full. The choice of divergence therefore matters. Forward Kullback–Leibler (KL) divergence (i.e., KL \operatorname{KL} (teacher ∥ \| student)) encourages the student to cover the teacher’s full range of responses. Reverse KL (i.e., KL \operatorname{KL} (student ∥ \| teacher)) instead allows a limited-capacity student to concentrate on teacher behaviors it can represent, while discouraging responses that are unlikely under the teacher. Reverse KL has shown empirical promise in on-policy distillation for large language models (LLMs), where the student generates responses and learns from the teacher’s action probability at the observed state ( Gu et al., 2024 ; Agarwal et al., 2024 ; Lu and Thinking Machines Lab, 2025 ) . Although the empirical results are promising, the optimal statistical guarantees for reverse-KL learning remain unclear. The statistical question depends first on what information the teacher provides. Some distillation methods only use the teacher’s probability on student-generated actions ( Lu and Thinking Machines Lab, 2025 ) , whereas recent studies report benefits from access to the teacher’s full action distribution ( Li et al., 2026b ; Yu et al., 2026 ; Fu et al., 2026 ) . Whether this richer form of teacher feedback improves statistical efficiency, and by how much, remains open. Moreover, reverse KL is evaluated under the student’s distribution, so training typically uses student-generated responses. It is therefore unclear whether learning from offline teacher-generated data can match or even improve on the statistical guarantees attainable from online student rollouts. To answer these questions, we study sequence-level reverse-KL learning with a student policy class that may not contain the teacher, allowing for misspecification . Our framework distinguishes two aspects of the learning process: who generates the training trajectories and what information the teacher provides along them. The trajectories come either from student policies chosen adaptively by the learner in the online setting, or from the teacher in the offline setting. With either data source, the teacher may reveal its entire action distribution at each visited state ( full feedback ) or only the probability of the observed action ( action feedback ). Across these four settings, we study how closely a learner can match the best student in its policy class for a given number of training trajectories. We give a rather complete picture for this problem. With full feedback, we establish the minimax-optimal guarantees for reverse-KL learning under a relative second-moment assumption. For the online setting, we first show that common local distillation losses can be suboptimal. These objectives, motivated by DAgger and on-policy distillation ( Ross et al., 2011 ; Lu and Thinking Machines Lab, 2025 ) , evaluate candidate policy on states generated by the rollout policies, including state that a candidate itself would rarely visit, which can distort policy rankings. Our algorithm ( Algorithm 1 ) corrects this mismatch by reweighting the observed prefix to account for each policy’s own generation behavior, attaining the optimal guarantee ( Section 3 ). For the offline setting, we develop a new algorithm ( Equation 12 ) that attains the same optimal guarantee from teacher-generated trajectories. With action feedback only, online learning can require substantially more samples than with full feedback ( Section 3.4 ). Yet under a trajectory likelihood-ratio bound, offline learning with action feedback can still obtain a comparable guarantee to full feedback learning ( Sections 3.4 and 4 ). These results show that richer feedback can improve online sample efficiency, while surprisingly optimal reverse-KL learning need not require online interaction. Formally, let π ⋆ \pi^{\star} be the teacher policy, Π \Pi be the student policy class, and P π P^{\pi} the sequence distribution generated by π \pi . Our guarantees take the form KL ( P π ^ ∥ P π ⋆ ) ≤ C app min π ∈ Π KL ( P π ∥ P π ⋆ ) + C est log ⁡ ( | Π | / δ ) T \operatorname{KL}(P^{\widehat{\pi}}\|P^{\pi^{\star}})\leq C_{\rm app}\min_{\pi\in\Pi}\operatorname{KL}(P^{\pi}\|P^{\pi^{\star}})+C_{\rm est}\frac{\log(|\Pi|/\delta)}{T} with probability at least 1 − δ 1-\delta , using T T complete episodes and returning π ^ ∈ Π \widehat{\pi}\in\Pi . Here C app C_{\rm app} (approximation factor) measures the approximation cost of competing with the best available student, and C est C_{\rm est} (estimation factor) controls the estimation error. At the minimax scale of C est C_{\rm est} , we characterize the smallest attainable C app C_{\rm app} . Table 1 summarizes the guarantees and separations. The assumptions hold for every π \pi and feasible trajectory τ \tau . The trajectory likelihood-ratio condition is stronger and implies the relative second moment condition with B = 4 ​ ( B ∞ + 1 ) B=4(B_{\infty}+1) ( Lemma D.1 ). Related work. Our closest theoretical predecessors Rohatgi et al. (2025) and Xu et al. (2026b) also study imitation learning under misspecification. Rohatgi et al. (2025) obtain constant approximation and estimation coefficients for learning trajectory Hellinger distance with computationally inefficient algorithms, and show that standard next-token prediction approaches (e.g. cross-entropy loss) must suffer an Ω ⁡ ( H ) \Omega(H) approximation factor where H H is the learning horizon. Xu et al. (2026b) establish a constant approximation factor for learning forward KL divergence under standard cross-entropy loss, but the estimation error scales with a boundedness factor. Both papers only study offline learning from teacher trajectories with action feedback. We study reverse-KL learning in both online and offline settings and characterize the statistical advantage of full feedback over action feedback. Appendix A provides further discussion of related work. 2 Problem formulation Notation. For a positive integer n n , write [ n ] = { 1 , … , n } [n]=\{1,\ldots,n\} . All logarithms are natural unless a base is displayed. We use x ∧ y = min ⁡ { x , y } x\wedge y=\min\{x,y\} , x + = max ⁡ { x , 0 } x_{+}=\max\{x,0\} , and 𝟏 ​ { E } \mathbf{1}\{E\} for the indicator of an event E E . The notation O O , Ω \Omega , and Θ \Theta denotes upper, lower, and two-sided bounds up to positive numerical factors, and ≲ \lesssim suppresses such an upper-bound factor. We write x ≍ y x\asymp y when both x ≲ y x\lesssim y and y ≲ x y\lesssim x . For distributions p , q p,q , write KL ( p ∥ q ) = ∑ z p ( z ) log ( p ( z ) / q ( z ) ) \operatorname{KL}(p\|q)=\sum_{z}p(z)\log(p(z)/q(z)) , where terms with p ⁡ ( z ) = 0 p(z)=0 equal zero and KL ( p ∥ q ) = + ∞ \operatorname{KL}(p\|q)=+\infty if p ⁡ ( z ) > 0 p(z)>0 and q ⁡ ( z ) = 0 q(z)=0 for some z z . Setting. We consider a reward-free Markov decision process with horizon H ≥ 1 H\geq 1 , discrete state space 𝒮 \mathcal{S} , action set 𝒜 \mathcal{A} , initial state distribution μ \mu , and transition kernel 𝖯 h ( ⋅ ∣ s , a ) \mathsf{P}_{h}(\cdot\mid s,a) . A Markov policy π = ( π h ) h = 1 H \pi=(\pi_{h})_{h=1}^{H} consists of maps π h : 𝒮 → Δ ⁡ ( 𝒜 ) \pi_{h}:\mathcal{S}\to\Delta(\mathcal{A}) , where Δ ⁡ ( 𝒜 ) = { p ∈ [ 0 , 1 ] | 𝒜 | : ∑ a ∈ 𝒜 p ⁡ ( a ) = 1 } \Delta(\mathcal{A})=\{p\in[0,1]^{|\mathcal{A}|}:\sum_{a\in\mathcal{A}}p(a)=1\} is the probability simplex over actions. We write π h ​ ( a ∣ s ) \pi_{h}(a\mid s) for the probability assigned to action a a at state s s . Let s h ∈ 𝒮 s_{h}\in\mathcal{S} and a h ∈ 𝒜 a_{h}\in\mathcal{A} denote the state and action at step h h . Under π \pi , an episode generates a trajectory τ = ( s 1 , a 1 , … , s H , a H ) ∈ 𝒯 = ( 𝒮 × 𝒜 ) H \tau=(s_{1},a_{1},\ldots,s_{H},a_{H})\in\mathcal{T}=(\mathcal{S}\times\mathcal{A})^{H} by sampling s 1 ∼ μ s_{1}\sim\mu , a h ∼ π h ( ⋅ ∣ s h ) a_{h}\sim\pi_{h}(\cdot\mid s_{h}) , and, for h < H h<H , s h + 1 ∼ 𝖯 h ( ⋅ ∣ s h , a h ) s_{h+1}\sim\mathsf{P}_{h}(\cdot\mid s_{h},a_{h}) . We write P π P^{\pi} for the trajectory distribution under policy π \pi , so P π ​ ( τ ) = μ ⁡ ( s 1 ) ​ ∏ h = 1 H π h ​ ( a h ∣ s h ) ​ ∏ h = 1 H − 1 𝖯 h ​ ( s h + 1 ∣ s h , a h ) . P^{\pi}(\tau)=\mu(s_{1})\prod_{h=1}^{H}\pi_{h}(a_{h}\mid s_{h})\prod_{h=1}^{H-1}\mathsf{P}_{h}(s_{h+1}\mid s_{h},a_{h}). Let ξ h = ( s 1 , a 1 , … , s h − 1 , a h − 1 , s h ) \xi_{h}=(s_{1},a_{1},\ldots,s_{h-1},a_{h-1},s_{h}) denote the prefix before action a h a_{h} . Its probability under π \pi is P π ​ ( ξ h ) = μ ⁡ ( s 1 ) ​ ∏ j = 1 h − 1 π j ​ ( a j ∣ s j ) ​ 𝖯 j ​ ( s j + 1 ∣ s j , a j ) . P^{\pi}(\xi_{h})=\mu(s_{1})\prod_{j=1}^{h-1}\pi_{j}(a_{j}\mid s_{j})\mathsf{P}_{j}(s_{j+1}\mid s_{j},a_{j}). The empty product equals one when h = 1 h=1 . The learner is given a finite policy class Π \Pi and seeks to imitate a fixed teacher π ⋆ \pi^{\star} . Define the local reverse KL between policy π \pi and π ⋆ \pi^{\star} at state s s and step h h by k h ( s ; π ) = KL ( π h ( ⋅ ∣ s ) ∥ π h ⋆ ( ⋅ ∣ s ) ) k_{h}(s;\pi)=\operatorname{KL}(\pi_{h}(\cdot\mid s)\|\pi_{h}^{\star}(\cdot\mid s)) . Our target is the trajectory reverse-KL risk , whose chain-rule decomposition is L ( π ) := KL ( P π ∥ P π ⋆ ) = 𝔼 P π [ ∑ h = 1 H k h ( s h ; π ) ] . L(\pi):=\operatorname{KL}(P^{\pi}\|P^{\pi^{\star}})=\mathbb{E}_{P^{\pi}}\big[\sum_{h=1}^{H}k_{h}(s_{h};\pi)\big]. Let L ⋆ = min π ∈ Π ⁡ L ⁡ ( π ) L^{\star}=\min_{\pi\in\Pi}L(\pi) . The setting is realizable when π ⋆ ∈ Π \pi^{\star}\in\Pi , giving L ⋆ = 0 L^{\star}=0 , and agnostic when the teacher need not belong to the class. Observation models. With a budget of T T complete episodes, we consider four observation models (see Table 1 ) that differ in their trajectory source and teacher feedback : • Trajectory source: In the online setting, at each round t ∈ [ T ] t\in[T] , the learner selects π t ∈ Π \pi_{t}\in\Pi based on past observations and executes it for a complete episode, obtaining τ t ∼ P π t \tau_{t}\sim P^{\pi_{t}} . In the offline setting, the learner receives independent teacher trajectories τ t ⋆ ∼ P π ⋆ \tau_{t}^{\star}\sim P^{\pi^{\star}} for t ∈ [ T ] t\in[T] . • Teacher feedback: At each visited state s h s_{h} , the learner receives one of two forms of teacher feedback. Full feedback reveals the teacher’s entire action distribution π h ⋆ ( ⋅ ∣ s h ) \pi_{h}^{\star}(\cdot\mid s_{h}) , whereas action feedback reveals only the probability π h ⋆ ​ ( a h ∣ s h ) \pi_{h}^{\star}(a_{h}\mid s_{h}) assigned to the observed action a h a_{h} . Either feedback model can accompany online or offline trajectories, and no feedback is available at unvisited states. Boundedness assumptions. Our full-feedback guarantees hold under a relative second-moment condition. For action feedback, we use a stronger trajectory likelihood-ratio bound. Assumption 2.1 (Relative second-moment bound) . There exists B ≥ 1 B\geq 1 such that, for every π ∈ Π \pi\in\Pi , 𝔼 τ ∼ P π [ ( ∑ h = 1 H KL ( π h ( ⋅ ∣ s h ) ∥ π h ⋆ ( ⋅ ∣ s h ) ) ) 2 ] ≤ B KL ( P π ∥ P π ⋆ ) < ∞ . \mathbb{E}_{\tau\sim P^{\pi}}\!\left[\left(\sum_{h=1}^{H}\operatorname{KL}\!\left(\pi_{h}(\cdot\mid s_{h})\,\middle\|\,\pi_{h}^{\star}(\cdot\mid s_{h})\right)\right)^{2}\right]\leq B\,\operatorname{KL}(P^{\pi}\|P^{\pi^{\star}})<\infty. By the KL chain rule, the average cumulative local KL under P π P^{\pi} equals the trajectory divergence KL ( P π ∥ P π ⋆ ) \operatorname{KL}(P^{\pi}\|P^{\pi^{\star}}) . Assumption 2.1 thus imposes a Bernstein-type moment condition , the second moment is controlled linearly by the mean under each candidate policy’s own trajectory distribution. Intuitively, trajectories with cumulative local KL much larger than B B can contribute only a small fraction of the average reverse KL. This condition is weaker than several uniform boundedness assumptions. For example, a uniform local KL bound k h ​ ( s , π ) ≤ G k_{h}(s;\pi)\leq G for all h , s , π h,s,\pi implies Assumption 2.1 with B = max ⁡ { 1 , H ​ G } B=\max\{1,HG\} . The trajectory likelihood-ratio bound in Assumption 2.2 below also implies Assumption 2.1 , with B = 4 ​ ( B ∞ + 1 ) B=4(B_{\infty}+1) . Section D.1 provides the precise implications and proofs. Proposition 4.3 and Theorem 3.5 show that, under Assumption 2.2 , offline action-feedback learning can require exponentially fewer episodes than online action-feedback learning in the worst case. 5 Conclusion We characterize how data source and teacher feedback shape reverse-KL learning under misspecification. For the online learning setting, we show the failure of common empirical algorithms and provide the first algorithm achieving the optimal guarantee under full feedback and a relative second-moment condition. We further show that full feedback can significantly improve online sample efficiency over action feedback. For the offline setting, we also establish algorithms with tight bounds, demonstrating that under a trajectory likelihood-ratio bound, teacher trajectories can avoid the additional sample cost of online learning with action feedback. Future work includes developing and empirically evaluating practical distillation algorithms based on our prefix reweighting and trajectory clipping mechanism, and determining the optimal statistical guarantees achievable by computationally efficient learners. Appendix A Related work Offline imitation learning theory Offline imitation learning asks what can be learned from a fixed set of expert demonstrations without further interaction. In the realizable setting, classical analyses of zero-one-loss behavior cloning relate action-prediction errors to compounding errors in task performance [ Ross and Bagnell, 2010 ] . Rajaraman et al. [2020] characterize minimax task-performance guarantees in finite-state MDPs, showing that error compounding can be unavoidable when dynamics are unknown. With known dynamics and a deterministic expert, improved dependence on the horizon is possible [ Rajaraman et al., 2021 ] . For general policy classes under realizability, Foster et al. [2024] show that log-loss behavior cloning admits horizon-free guarantees when the cumulative reward range and policy-class complexity are controlled. Additional offline data provide another source of information: MILO learns a dynamics model from auxiliary transition data and mitigates covariate shift when those data sufficiently cover the expert’s behavior [ Chang et al., 2021 ] . Our offline learners instead use teacher trajectories and the specified probability feedback, without auxiliary transition data. When the student policy class is not expressive enough to cover the teacher, the question becomes how closely a learner can compete with the best available policy. Due to the different directions in forward and reverse KL, we assume the teacher can cover any student, whereas Xu et al. [2026b] assumes any student can cover the teacher. Teacher coverage is more natural for distillation because a limited-capacity student may concentrate on teacher-supported behaviors without representing the teacher’s entire range of behaviors. Interactive imitation learning A student may visit states rarely represented in teacher demonstrations, especially after making a mistake [ Ross and Bagnell, 2010 ] . DAgger obtains expert supervision on these states and reduces imitation to no-regret online learning [ Ross et al., 2011 ] . Li and Zhang [2024] give an oracle-efficient agnostic algorithm with access to exploratory state samples. Its comparator measures local imitation error on states visited during training; ours evaluates each candidate under its own trajectory law. Thus a small online regret alone does not imply our reverse-KL oracle bound. Several works identify conditions under which interaction improves imitation-learning performance. Espinosa-Dice et al. [2025] avoid quadratic error compounding under a completeness condition on the policy class. Zhang et al. [2026] identify an offline information bottleneck under misspecification even at horizon one. Sriraman et al. [2026] establish an exponential benefit from interaction with a noisy expert when performance is measured against a clean expert. Viano et al. [2026] obtain efficient on-policy imitation when the expert’s Q-function, rather than its policy, is realizable. These guarantees concern different targets and assumptions from our comparison of online and offline reverse-KL learning rates. Language-model distillation Building on knowledge and policy distillation [ Hinton et al., 2015 , Rusu et al., 2016 ] , language-model distillation can use teacher-generated responses [ Kim and Rush, 2016 ] or student-generated responses [ Lin et al., 2020 , Agarwal et al., 2024 , Li et al., 2026a ] , with forward KL and reverse KL as common losses. Beyond the standard losses, Wu et al. [2025] propose an adaptive combination of these two losses. Ko et al. [2024] propose skew KL losses that compare a distribution with a mixture of teacher and student distributions, while Ko et al. [2025] use a contrastive objective to increase the likelihood of teacher responses and decrease that of student responses. Gu et al. [2024] develop policy-gradient updates for sequence-level reverse KL, using returns based on accumulated future teacher-to-student log likelihood ratios. These returns allow later predictions to influence updates to earlier actions. The feedback available at each training recipe is a separate choice. Lu and Thinking Machines Lab [2025] use teacher probabilities for sampled tokens, Xu et al. [2026a] use full next-token distributions, and Fu et al. [2026] , Yu et al. [2026] incorporate information about teacher-preferred alternatives. Our full-versus-action-feedback comparison isolates the statistical value of the available information by comparing the best attainable rates under each feedback model.
